metaTitle: Mobile App Design Agency: iOS & Android UX | Designit
metaDescription: Mobile app design for iOS and Android: research, flows, interface design, platform conventions, offline and slow-network states, prototypes and handoff.
h1: Mobile app design for products people open every day
subtitle: A mobile app gets seconds of attention, on a small screen, often on an unreliable connection. We design apps around the one or two jobs people open them for, and make those jobs fast, forgiving and native to each platform.
serviceDescription: Mobile app UX and UI design for iOS, iPadOS and Android: research, flows, interface design that follows platform conventions, offline and low-bandwidth states, prototyping, usability testing and developer handoff.
audienceType: Consumer and B2B product teams building or redesigning mobile apps
author: Designit
aiAnswerTargets: How do you design a mobile app for iOS and Android?
Should iOS and Android apps look the same?
How much does mobile app design cost?

cta.heading: Let's look at your app on a real phone
cta.body: Send us your app or prototype. In 30 minutes we'll walk the core flow on a mid-range device and tell you where people are likely to drop.

items.title: Onboarding asks before it gives
items.body: Account creation, permissions and preferences before the app has shown any value.

items.title: Permission prompts at the wrong moment
items.body: Notifications and location requested on first launch, without context, and refused for good.

items.title: Navigation built for a desktop product
items.body: Too many tabs, deep menus and actions out of thumb reach.

items.title: Forms that fight the keyboard
items.body: Wrong input types, tiny targets and validation that only fires after submit.

items.title: Fragile on real networks
items.body: Blank screens on a weak connection, lost input on a dropped request, and no offline state at all.

items.title: Core flows
items.body: The one or two jobs people open the app for, made as short and forgiving as possible.

items.title: Onboarding and activation
items.body: A first session that delivers value before asking for commitment, with permissions requested in context.

items.title: Navigation and information architecture
items.body: Structures that fit a thumb and a short attention span, tested with real users.

items.title: Interface design across states
items.body: Loading, empty, error, offline and permission-denied states designed, not left to engineering.

items.title: Tablet and large screens
items.body: Layouts that use iPad and tablet space properly rather than stretching the phone design.

items.title: Design systems for mobile
items.body: Components and tokens shared across iOS and Android while respecting each platform.

sections.heading: Designing for real devices and networks
paras: Much of the audience in the markets we work in uses mid-range Android hardware on unreliable connections. That shapes real decisions: image weight, how much state lives on the device, what works offline, and whether an animation is worth its frame cost.
We review designs on representative devices and throttled networks, not only on a designer's laptop, because that is where most mobile usability problems hide.

items.title: Research

items.title: Flows and architecture

sections.heading: How much does mobile app design cost?
sections.answer: Mobile app design is quoted against a written scope. The main drivers are the number of core flows, whether you need both iOS and Android designs, and how much research and testing the product needs.
body: Other factors: tablet layouts, offline behaviour, accessibility requirements, a mobile design system, and the depth of build support. For more context, read the cost of UI/UX design for a mobile app in India.

faq.q: Should our iOS and Android apps look the same?
faq.a: Your brand, content and core flows should be consistent; navigation patterns, controls and system behaviour should feel native to each platform. People notice when an app ignores the conventions of their phone.

faq.q: Do you design for tablets and iPad?
faq.a: Yes. Larger screens deserve layouts that use the space, such as split views and side panels, rather than a stretched phone design.

faq.q: Can you redesign an existing app without disrupting current users?
faq.a: Yes. We start from analytics and user research on the current app, keep what people rely on, and sequence changes so existing users are not forced to relearn everything at once.

faq.q: Do you design for offline and low-bandwidth use?
faq.a: As a default case. We design loading, partial and offline states explicitly and test on throttled connections.
We design and specify the app and support your engineers or development partner through build with design QA. Development itself sits with your team or partner.

faq.q: How long does mobile app design take?
faq.a: It depends on the number of flows and platforms. A single core flow can be designed in a few weeks; a full app across iOS and Android with a design system takes longer, and you get written dates before we start.
